turns.prompt_text: What kind of screws do sunglasses use or bolts
turns.response_html:
Most sunglasses and eyeglasses use specialized, miniature fasteners designed to fit into narrow hinges and thin frames. Depending on the material and design of your glasses, you’ll usually find one of the following:

1. Standard Eyeglass Screws

These are the most common fasteners. They are typically made of stainless steel or nickel silver to resist corrosion from sweat and skin oils.

  • Thread Sizes: The most common sizes are M1.0, M1.2, and M1.4.
  • Drive Types: Most use a small Phillips or Flathead drive.
  • Self-Tapping Screws: Some plastic frames use self-tapping screws that cut their own threads into the acetate as they are driven in.

2. Spring Hinge Screws

If your sunglasses have "flex" or spring hinges, the screws are often slightly longer and may have a tapered point (called a pilot point or "easy-start" tip). This helps align the tensioned spring mechanism with the screw hole during assembly.

3. Bolts and Nuts (Rimless Frames)

Rimless or "three-piece" sunglasses often don't use traditional screw holes in the frame. Instead, they use:

  • Longer Bolts: These pass through a hole drilled directly into the lens.
  • Hex Nuts: A tiny hexagonal nut (usually 2.0mm or 2.25mm) secures the bolt on the back side of the lens.
  • Compression Sleeves: Some modern rimless designs (like Silhouette) skip screws entirely and use plastic "bushings" or sleeves that compression-fit into the lens.

4. Torx or Star Screws

High-end performance or "tactical" brands (like Oakley or Spy) often use Torx (star-shaped) screws, typically size T3, T4, or T5. These are used because they are harder to strip and allow for higher torque during factory assembly.

Pro Tip: If you're replacing a lost screw, most "universal" repair kits found at drugstores work for about 80% of frames, but they often struggle with spring hinges. If the hole doesn't align, try using a safety pin to pull the hinge mechanism forward before inserting the screw.

turns.prompt_text: Can I buy a variety pack of these small M1 and 1.2 and M 1.4 screws
turns.response_html:
Yes, you can easily find variety packs that include M1.0, M1.2, and M1.4 screws. These are commonly sold as "Eyeglass Repair Kits" or "Miniature Screw Assortments" and typically include hundreds of pieces across various lengths and head styles (Phillips or Flathead).

Best Miniature Screw Variety Packs

For a comprehensive selection, these kits provide a wide range of the specific sizes you need, often including matching nuts and a miniature screwdriver.

  • 600pcs Tiny Micro Assortment Screws: This is a highly practical kit for repairs, featuring M1.0, M1.2, and M1.4 sizes. It includes 12 different variations of screws and nuts, ensuring you have the right length for standard frames or nose pads. It also comes with a mini cross screwdriver.
  • 601x Small Screws and Nuts Set: A large variety pack made of stainless steel for rust resistance. It covers the M1.0 to M1.6 range and is organized in a transparent plastic box with a specification label for quick identification.
  • Lyjee 1000pcs Miniature Phillips Screws: If you only need Phillips heads, this kit is ideal. It contains 1,000 pieces across 10 sizes, specifically focusing on M1, M1.2, and M1.4 diameters with varying lengths from 3mm to 6mm.

Specialized and Precision Kits

If you are looking for specific colors to match your frames or need high-precision tools included, these options offer a more tailored approach.

  • 150pcs Gold Phillips Head Micro Screw Set: Best for gold-toned metal frames. It includes M1.2 and M1.4 screws and comes with specialized accessories like a cleaning cloth and tweezers to handle the tiny parts.
  • 11Pcs Small Screwdriver Set: While this is primarily a tool set, it is the perfect companion for a variety pack. It includes precision drivers for 1.0mm, 1.2mm, and 1.4mm heads, which are essential for driving these miniature screws without stripping them.
